name: Binge US
_comment_group: A show under the Snapchat heading, built to Noisy Dish's brief and
departing from it in one place: what the card is MADE of.
Everything that makes this a Snapchat pack is Hall of Femme's and is
stated in the same two references - the frame fetch, the vertical
output, the transcription, the rewrite, and how the caption is set.
Noisy Dish was the first pack here to say the still is a card lying on
something rather than the surface itself. This one keeps the card and
takes the photograph out of it. What is left is a sheet of paper, and
the picture reaches the frame twice around it: blurred and enlarged
UNDER the card, where it is the colour of the margin rather than
anything anyone reads, and cut to the person ON the card, where it is
the only sharp thing in the frame.
That is the whole design, and it is one idea rather than three effects:
a still cannot be both the background and the subject at full strength,
so it is spent entirely on the subject and the background is made out
of what is left over. It is also why the type can be absolute black
with nothing behind it - there is no photograph under the letters to
hold them off, only paper.
First pack under this heading to compose from a cutout. Nothing about
the frame fetch changes for it: a capture slot is an ordinary frame
record and /cutout-frame takes it like any other (see
api._capture_frames_sync). The face-fill penalty Laugh Society has to
turn off is not in this path at all - a capture run picks its frames on
whole-picture quality through frame_grab and never reaches the
face-based scorer - so there is nothing here to turn off.
Written as its own folder rather than as an override of a sibling, for
the reason content/README.md gives: a channel is a folder that gets
dropped in. The prose below points at noisy-dish and laugh-society-1
wherever the reasoning is theirs and states its own where this pack
decides something.

that restates a shared answer is a pack that can be missing a piece of
_comment_framing: The shared answer, unchanged. A cutout channel elsewhere in this app
states a framing profile of its own because the crop it never shows
would otherwise decide which frames it gets; here the crop is chosen by
the capture run rather than by the face scorer, so there is no such
decision to correct. See the group note above.
_comment_photo: The card, and what is under it. Noisy Dish's geometry to the pixel -
the same 85% and the same 13px of rounding, for the reasons its own
`photo` note gives - and neither of its two gradients.
`fill` is the departure and it is the channel. The card is a sheet of
warm off-white paper and the still is not drawn on it, which is what
makes everything else here possible: the subject stands on a known
colour instead of on an unknown photograph, and so does the type. A
printed cream rather than pure white, because white is what the type is
NOT - a card at #FFFFFF under black capitals is a screenshot of a
document, and #F5F2E3 is paper, which is what a news card is pretending
to be.
The backdrop is the frame's own still, cropped to its middle half and
blurred by 30px - see `photo.backdrop` in js/channels.js for what the
two numbers do and why the crop happens before the blur. It is not
decoration and it is not a colour picked to go with the card: it is the
one ground that is different on every thumbnail and right on every
thumbnail, because it is made of the picture the thumbnail is of. A
flat colour in the margin would have to be chosen once for a channel
whose stills are a nightclub, a courtroom and a beach.
0.5 rather than the whole frame, and the reason is what a blur does
rather than what a crop does. A 30px blur spreads every piece of detail
across 30px of the result, so what survives it is whatever was already
larger than that; on a 540-wide still at full size very little is, and
the margin comes back an even grey carrying the picture's average
colour. At half the frame every shape is twice the size going in, and
what comes out still has the picture's lighting and its large masses in
it - which is the difference between a soft version of the photograph
and a smear of its mean.
30 rather than less, though, and that is the other end of the same
trade. The margin is 41px wide down the sides: anything still legible
in a band that narrow competes with the card, and the one thing this
ground must never do is look like a second picture.
No tint, and it is not an omission. A tint is what ties a photograph to
the ground it is lying on, and the thing lying on this ground is not a
photograph - it is a flat colour that was never going to be mistaken
for one. Laid on anyway it would only be a wash of colour over the
paper, and the paper is the brand.
_comment_cutout: The person, cut out of the frame whole by the backend (see
/cutout-frame and backend/background_remover.py) and stood on the card.
The fit and the zoom range are Laugh Society's, number for number, and
deliberately so - the two channels ask the same thing of a subject,
which is that they arrive somewhere sensible and are then composed by
hand. Its own `cutout` note carries the reasoning for every one of
those and is worth reading before any of them is changed; what follows
is only what this channel had to decide for itself.
Two of them are this channel's own and are where it parts company with
the pack it copied.
anchorX 0.5 puts the subject in the MIDDLE. Laugh Society stands them
in the left half because the title is in the right half, and that is a
composition this channel does not have: the caption is above them, at
the top of the card, across its full width. With the type out of the
way sideways there is nothing for a subject standing to one side to be
beside, and an off-centre figure on a symmetrical card reads as a
layout that slipped rather than one that was chosen.
It moves the room without resizing it, which is the reason it is a key
of its own rather than fitWidthRatio 1. The subject still arrives
fitted to half the frame's width - 270px of a 540-wide canvas - and
that half still leaves air around them. Fitted to the WHOLE width they
would arrive height-limited instead on any full-length shot, standing
nearly 900px tall on a 960px canvas, which is a figure reaching up
through the caption and out of the top of the card.
And there is exactly one of them, on every slot. Laugh Society offers
the subject twice and three times on half its grid, because a comic
shown three times in three poses is a look that show is FOR. A news
card is not: it is one person, one moment, one headline, and a second
copy of the same face on it reads as a mistake in the cut rather than
as a device. Said by leaving copiesBySlot out rather than by writing a
list of ones - absent means one (see editor.copiesForSlot), and
copyScale and copyOffsetGap go with it because they exist only to
place a figure that is not there.
That also takes a real cost off every thumbnail. Each extra figure is
a separate restoration of a separate moment on the one GPU (see
editor.cutOut, which runs them in sequence), so a grid that used to
cost twenty cut-outs plus twenty more for the doubled and tripled
slots now costs twenty.
bottomRatio 0.925 stands them on the CARD's bottom edge rather than
the canvas's, and it is the one number here that is neither Laugh
Society's nor arrived at from scratch. It is read off `photo` above:
the card is fillRatio of the canvas and centred, so its foot sits at
(1 + 0.85) / 2 of the height - 888px of 960 - and the two numbers have
to be changed together. A card resized without this is a figure
standing in mid-air or buried, and nothing in the app will say so.
It was Laugh Society's 1 until it was asked to line up, which stood
them on the canvas's own edge and let the figure cross the card's foot
and finish on the blurred ground. The argument for that was that a
subject breaking out of the card reads as a person in front of a
graphic, where feet tucked inside a rounded rectangle read as a smaller
photograph pasted into a larger one. What it did NOT survive is that
the card here is a solid colour and not a picture: a figure whose feet
stop 72px below the one hard edge in the composition reads as a layer
that missed its mark rather than as depth. Standing them ON that edge
is the alignment the card is asking for, and the overhang is still
available to anyone who wants it - the figure is draggable and
resizable from wherever it lands, as it is everywhere else.
The shadow is where the two Laugh Society packs disagree, so it is the
one thing here that had to be chosen rather than copied. They share the
blur (24) and the alpha (0.8) and differ on the throw: 24px on the
stage channel, 6 on the other.
6, and for the ground rather than for the figure. A 24px throw says
the person is standing well in front of what is behind them, which is
true of a lit stage and false of a sheet of paper. At 6 the shadow
stays under the figure and does what it is actually here for:
separating a cut edge from a flat colour.
It was also chosen against the overhang this pack used to have, where
the figure crossed the card's foot and the shadow had to fall on two
surfaces at once - at 24 the part below that edge threw a hard
diagonal across the blurred ground. That case is gone now that the
feet land on the card's edge (see bottomRatio above), but the number
is kept, because the first reason was always the load-bearing one and
a user who drags a figure down still gets the overhang back.
overTitle is this channel's own, and it is the whole of why the caption
can sit where it does - see the layout note below.
_comment_title: Anton, absolute black, at the top of the card, under the figure.
Everything else about how a caption is set under this heading - the
size, where the lines break, the capitals, the character count, that
the user can drag the block off a face - is the Snapchat caption design
and is stated once in content/presets/snapchat-caption.json.

_comment_face: Anton. A grotesque with almost no counter and almost no
sidebearing, which is the face a headline is set in when the
headline is the point - it holds a whole sentence across 90% of a
540-wide frame at 40px without the preset having to shrink
It has a lower case, unlike the Bebas its neighbour is set in, so
the preset's capitals are a transformation laid over the face here
rather than the face's own answer. That is the right way round for
this channel: the capitals are the caption's decision and not the
type's, and a pack that later wants sentence case has one key to
change instead of a different font to find.
_comment_color: Absolute black, on every frame, with no palette offered beside it.
Black is not the default that white would have been - it is what
the card being paper makes possible. Every other channel under this
heading sets light letters because there is a photograph somewhere
under them; this one has a known colour under every letter of every
caption, and on #F5F2E3 the strongest thing a word can be is
Absolute rather than a soft near-black. A near-black is what you
reach for to stop type vibrating against pure white, and this is
not pure white - the card is already warm and already a step down
from it, so the pair is a printed one and #000000 is simply the
No second colour, for the reason Noisy Dish gives: the colour in
this channel is the ground, and a palette in the type would be a
third thing competing with the paper and the blurred margin. Hall
of Femme hands two of its colours to the user because the PAIRING
of card and letters is what that show is; here the card is one
colour on every frame, so there is no pairing to offer.
_comment_panel: None. The preset's card is exactly what this channel already has
and cannot have twice: the still has been taken out of the photo
card and replaced by a flat colour, so the caption is ALREADY on a
solid ground somebody picked. A second slab laid on it would be a
background on a background, in a colour that has to either match
the paper - and be invisible - or not, and be a patch.
Dropping it drops the preset's shadow with it, which is correct and
not a loss: that shadow lifts a card off a photograph, and there is
no photograph here for anything to be lifted off. The preset's own
`shadow: null` for the letters stands unchanged too - black on
cream needs nothing under it, and the sibling that puts an opaque
shadow back does so because its letters stand on the amber foot of
Stated as null rather than left out, because the preset states one
and a pack that says nothing inherits it whole.
_comment_highlight: None, and here it is a brand decision rather than a consequence.
A highlight under this heading is one of three things: another
colour, another cut of the face, or a box. All three are available
- Anton is one weight, but a colour or a box on cream would work
perfectly well - and none is wanted. This caption is a news
headline, and a headline with one word picked out in a second
colour is an advertisement; the whole line is the emphasis.
The word buttons in the panel stay where they are and go dead, with
a tooltip saying whose decision that was (see
editor.renderWordButtons) - a live button that produced no visible
change would read as the app ignoring the click.

_comment: The preset's block, moved to the other end of the frame.
vAlign top with topRatio 0.125 is the mirror of the preset's own
bottom margin, and it lands in the same place measured from the
other edge: 120px down a 960-tall frame, which is 48px inside
the card's top edge at fillRatio 0.85. Noisy Dish's caption sits
48px up from the card's foot for the same reason, so the two
channels put their type the same distance into the card and
differ only in which way up.
Measured off the FRAME rather than off the card, like every
other layout number here. That is a relation worth knowing
before either number is touched: shrinking the card moves its
top edge DOWN while the type stays where it is, so a smaller
fillRatio eventually puts the first line on the blurred ground
above the card. Nothing breaks when it does - the type just
stops being on paper, which is the whole design.
A caption that runs long grows DOWNWARD from here, which is the
other half of why this end of the frame is the right one. The
subject stands on the bottom edge, so the two things grow
towards each other from opposite ends and a long caption meets
the figure rather than being pushed off the card by it - and
where they meet, the figure is in front (see `overTitle`
above). The type passing behind a shoulder is the picture this
channel is for; the type sliding off the paper would not be.
Everything else is the preset's and is not restated: the size,
the width, the character count, the four lines, the freeform
box. Only the end of the frame has changed.
